title: Gideon's Three Hundred
text:
The Midianites and their allies had been raiding Israel for years, and now their vast army lay camped in the valley of Jezreel. Gideon gathered thirty two thousand men against them. But, the book of Judges says, God told him the army was too large: if they won, Israel would boast that it had saved itself.

So Gideon announced that anyone who was afraid could go home. Twenty two thousand left. Ten thousand remained, still too many. Gideon led them down to the water to drink. Most knelt and put their faces to the water. Three hundred scooped up water with their hands and lapped it. Those three hundred he kept, and he sent the rest home.

That night Gideon crept down to the edge of the enemy camp with his servant Purah and overheard a soldier telling a dream about a loaf of barley bread that tumbled into the camp and knocked a tent flat. His comrade said it could only mean Gideon's sword.

Gideon divided his men into three companies and gave each man a ram's horn trumpet and an empty jar with a torch hidden inside. In the middle of the night they surrounded the camp. At his signal they blew the horns, smashed the jars, held up the blazing torches and shouted. In the dark and confusion, the Midianites turned their swords on each other and fled.
lesson: A smaller, committed team can beat a larger one when it chooses the moment, uses surprise and makes the enemy's own size and confusion work against it.
date: ancient Israelite tradition, set c. 12th century BC
caveat: The account is from the book of Judges, whose stories are not independently attested.
